The World Bible

Everything below is the scaffolding under THE WAKING DEPTH — the notes Maren kept pinned over her desk while she wrote it. None of it is required to win the game. All of it is true inside the game. Spoilers for the ending live at the very bottom, behind a fold.

Cormorant Light

Cormorant Light stands on a fist of black granite a mile and a quarter off the village of Cape Wrack, on a stretch of coast the old charts simply mark foul ground. It was raised in 1891 by the Wrack Harbour Trust, after the third winter in a row took a herring fleet with all hands and the Trust could no longer pretend the losses were ordinary weather. The tower is granite to the gallery and cast iron above, sixty-one feet from doorstep to lamp, with a first-order Fresnel lens that throws a single white flash every fifteen seconds — or did, until last autumn, when the flashes stopped and nobody could say exactly when.

The light was never automated. Every other lamp on the coast went to clockwork and then to electricity and then to a man in an office watching a screen. Not Cormorant. The Trust paid, quietly and without explanation, to keep a living keeper on the rock through every reform, every budget, every century. The keepers were always from the same handful of families. They were always, the records show, women. And they were always, eventually, the last of their line.

The keepers

  • Ailsa Crann (kept 1891–1934) — lit the lamp the first night. Left a single line in the dedication that every keeper since has signed beneath.
  • Morag Dunleavy (1934–1969) — began the practice of papering over the quarters' one window. "Never the sea," she wrote. "Not while you sleep."
  • Theodora Vane (1969–1998) — added the regulator valve to the lamp, and the cabinet to the watch room, and the lock to the cabinet.
  • Greer Holloway (1998–2025) — your grandmother. Kept the watch forty years. Stopped writing letters one autumn. The county says she drowned. The county was not on the rock.

The words on the door

Above the lighthouse door, carved deep enough to outlast the lichen, are three words: WE KEEP THE DARK. The village has spent a hundred and thirty years gently correcting visitors who misread it — surely it means the light; a lighthouse keeps the light. Somebody, more than once, has taken a chisel to it and tried to make it say so. The stone refuses.

It means exactly what it says. The keepers of Cormorant Light have never been in the business of holding back the dark. They have been in the business of keeping it — the way you keep a bee, a vow, or a dangerous animal you have agreed, for everyone's sake, to feed.

The thing in the deep

The keepers' journals never name it. They call it the Watcher, or simply company. What can be reconstructed: something very large and very old lives in the cold trench off the foul ground, and it is drawn — the way a moth is drawn, the way a lonely dog is drawn — to warmth, to motion, to a steady light circling on the water. While the lamp turns, the thing stays down. It has a fire to watch. It has somewhere to belong.

When the lamp goes dark, it does not rage. It does something far worse: it comes looking for the next warm thing. The herring fleets, the old charts' foul ground, the families that always end with a single daughter — these are the receipts for every night, across a hundred and thirty years, that the lamp was nearly allowed to fail. Greer understood this better than anyone before her. It is why she never let the light go out. It is, the game suggests, why she could not let herself leave.

The geography of the tower

You'll learn this by walking it, but here is the shape of the rock: the jetty where you tie up, the leaning boathouse to its west, and the shore path climbing north to the barred door. Inside, the flooded foyer opens west to the cold kitchen and up the spiral stair to your grandmother's quarters. Above the quarters: the instrument-lined watch room, and at the very top, behind the storm-glass, the lamp room and its great sleeping eye.

The game is about ten rooms, a handful of objects, and one long night. It can be finished in well under an hour. It is meant to be played in one sitting, ideally with the lights off.

Themes & intent

We wrote THE WAKING DEPTH about inherited duty — the jobs we are born into without consent, the love that is indistinguishable from a trap, and the strange tenderness of caretaking a thing that would destroy you if you ever stopped. The lighthouse is the obvious metaphor and we are not embarrassed by it. The real question the game puts to you is small and quiet and arrives only at the top of the stairs: now that you know what the watch costs, and what it keeps at bay — do you light it anyway?

The ending, explained (full spoilers)

To win, you relight the lamp — fuel it with the oil can, fit the regulator valve handle recovered from the watch-room cabinet, and strike a match. The light wakes, the lens throws it across the water, and the pale enormous shape beneath the storm-glass settles back into the deep, content, the way a great dog settles by a fire it trusts will not go out.

You sign your name beneath your grandmother's in the logbook. You inherit the watch. It is, deliberately, an ambiguous victory: you have saved the coast, and you have also just agreed to spend the rest of your life as a candle for a god, exactly as four women before you did. THE WAKING DEPTH calls this winning. Whether you agree is, we hope, the thing you carry out of the room.
